analysis.one_liner: Bans brokerages and investment firms from forcing customers into arbitration or waiving class-action lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The Investor Choice Act never got a committee vote or a House floor vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar brokers, dealers, investment advisers, and public companies from writing contracts that force investors to settle disputes in arbitration instead of court, or that make investors give up the right to join class-action lawsuits. It would also void those clauses in agreements investors already signed, except for cases already in arbitration. It was introduced by Rep. Bill Foster and six Democratic colleagues, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Retail investors — the ordinary people with brokerage accounts, retirement savings, or advisory relationships. If defrauded, they could choose to sue in court or join a class action instead of being locked into private, industry-run arbitration where discovery is limited and results are hard to appeal. Shareholders of public companies would also gain, since companies could no longer write bylaws or shareholder contracts forcing arbitration.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retail investors with brokerage or retirement accounts

how_it_helps.text: Lets investors choose: it makes it unlawful for brokers, dealers, funding portals, and municipal securities dealers to require arbitration, restrict the choice of forum, or bar class actions in agreements about future disputes, so a defrauded investor can go to court instead.

Applies to deals already signed: provisions in existing customer agreements that would be banned going forward are declared void, so current account holders are not stuck with old clauses — except where arbitration had already started before the law passed.

Extends the same protection to company shareholders: public companies could no longer mandate arbitration in their bylaws or in contracts with shareholders, because the SEC could refuse to register securities and exchanges could refuse to list securities of companies that do.
Keeps the same rules for investment advisers, closing the parallel loophole in the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 so advisory clients get the same choice of forum as brokerage customers.

analysis.who_pays: Broker-dealers, investment advisers, and public companies. They would face more lawsuits, class actions, and settlements, and would lose the control and predictability of forcing disputes into a private arbitration system run largely by the securities industry. Some of those litigation costs would likely show up in customer fees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Broker-dealers, investment advisers, and public companies

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves arbitration available only after a dispute actually arises, so firms lose the faster, lower-cost private process they prefer, and the added expense of defending suits in court — including class actions — could be passed on to customers through fees.
It applies retroactively, voiding clauses in agreements millions of investors already signed (except cases already in arbitration), which invites legal fights over the meaning of old contracts.

An honest supporter would concede that class actions often deliver small payments to individual investors and large fees to lawyers, while industry arbitration under FINRA rules can be quicker and cheaper for a straightforward claim — which is why the bill keeps arbitration as a voluntary option once a dispute exists rather than abolishing it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and goes to ordinary investors: the right to take a fraud claim to a public court with normal rules of evidence and appeal, instead of a private forum chosen by the firm being accused. The costs — higher litigation expense for firms and some transitional legal uncertainty — are real but limited, and the bill preserves arbitration for anyone who still prefers it once a dispute arises. On balance the protections outweigh the costs; the main reason it did not advance was not a documented flaw but the lack of any committee action at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, so it died quietly when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Foster introduced the Investor Choice Act on January 31, 2024, joined by five Democratic colleagues, and it was referred the same day to the House Financial Services Committee.
The complete action history shows exactly two entries — introduction and the committee referral — with no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action at any point.
The bill sat in committee for the rest of the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025, so it never received a vote in either chamber and expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broker-dealers, investment advisers, and public companies are better off: they keep the ability to write mandatory arbitration and class-action waiver clauses into customer and shareholder agreements, and defrauded investors remain limited to the industry's own arbitration system.

for.name: Rep. Bill Foster
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled five cosponsors; the bill was referred to his own committee.

for.name: Reps. Jan Schakowsky, Sean Casten, Gregory Meeks, Nydia Velázquez, and Madeleine Dean
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction; all six sponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership (Chair Patrick McHenry)
against.role: Chair of the committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill with no committee action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Securities industry (broker-dealers and investment advisers)
against.role: Businesses whose standard customer contracts would be restricted
against.what_they_did: Industry groups have consistently opposed mandatory-arbitration bans; no industry opposition activity appears in the congressional record for this bill.

sides.party_line_note: All seven original sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored; the Republican-controlled Financial Services Committee took no action, and no vote was ever recorded.

industries.note: These firms currently write mandatory arbitration and class-action waiver clauses into nearly all customer agreements, funneling disputes into private arbitration. The bill would strip that power, exposing them to court suits and class actions they can currently block — their cost is investors' recovered access to court.

Issuers could no longer put mandatory arbitration clauses in bylaws or shareholder agreements, and companies that did could be barred from listing or registering their securities. This closes the door on a practice some companies have tried in their charter documents.

industries.industry: FINRA and the securities arbitration system
industries.note: The industry-run arbitration forum would lose its captive pipeline of mandatory cases, since investors could take disputes to court instead. Arbitration would remain available, but only if the investor chooses it after a dispute arises.
